title: Europe confident its rules can thwart rogue AI
content:
Europe confident its rules can thwart rogue AI
European Union (EU) rules setting guardrails on AI use adopted by the bloc two years ago are more than capable of tackling rogue agents, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Reuters on Friday (local time).
There are mounting concerns worldwide triggered by recent incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic, sparking fears that rogue AI systems may slip beyond human control.
The EU's AI Act, which regulates the use of the technology based on the level of risk, is seen as embodying the world's strictest rules on artificial intelligence technology.
"We see that the safety and security of very capable models is a very hot topic internationally and we in Europe are well equipped for that," Virkkunen said in an interview.
"We have our AI Act in place and the AI Act covers the whole life cycle of these models," she added.
Regulators are providing guidance to companies on how to evaluate their models and how much time to allocate for this and would also factor in recommendations from a scientific panel of 60 AI experts from universities and institutions, she said.
Virkkunen dismissed criticism from some companies that the bloc's AI rules are already outdated.
"Our legislators and decision makers, I think that they have been taking into account very well already the coming developments, for example how they saw that the risks have to be assessed and external experts have to be used and they have to continue monitoring the models," she said.
The European Commission sent requests for information in late August to more than 30 AI companies asking for details of their safety and security measures and followed up with questions about their transparency and copyright obligations.
Such requests can lead to investigations that could result in fines of as much as 7 percent of a company's global annual turnover.
The Commission did not name the companies it had approached.
Virkkunen said she is now assessing the responses.
Asked about Chinese AI startups, Virkkunen said the Commission had "also sent requests for information to them", adding that the "most capable models" now in the markets were from the United States and China.
"I think that all these capable models, of course they are posing new kinds of risks that we have to be aware of," she said.
On whether the bloc should impose a digital levy which would fall mainly on big US tech companies, Virkkunen said the ball was in the court of EU governments which are now discussing new sources of financing for the EU budget for 2028 to 2034.
- Reuters

report.summary: EU tech chief says the bloc's AI Act can handle rogue AI amid global safety concerns, citing risk-based rules and expert oversight.
report.background: The EU adopted its AI Act two years ago as the world's strictest risk-based framework for artificial intelligence. It imposes obligations according to risk, from minimal to unacceptable, and covers the full model life cycle. Global anxiety has risen after recent incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic raised fears of rogue AI beyond human control. In late August, the European Commission asked more than 30 AI companies for details on safety, security, transparency and copyright, with potential fines up to 7 percent of global turnover. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen says these tools can handle emerging risks, while critics argue the rules may already be outdated. The bloc is also questioning Chinese AI firms and debating a digital levy.
key_points: The EU's AI Act regulates artificial intelligence by risk level and covers the full life cycle of models. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen says this makes Europe well equipped to handle rogue or highly capable AI, rejecting claims that the bloc's rules are already outdated.

The European Commission sent requests for information to more than 30 AI companies in late August, asking about safety, security, transparency and copyright. Non-compliance can trigger investigations and fines of up to 7 percent of a company's global annual turnover. Virkkunen is now assessing the responses.

A scientific panel of 60 AI experts from universities and institutions will help regulators evaluate models and decide how much time companies should spend on testing. The EU says it will continue monitoring models, aiming to combine legislation with external technical expertise as AI capabilities evolve.

Recent incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic have intensified worldwide fears that rogue AI systems could slip beyond human control. Virkkunen says the most capable models now come from the United States and China, and all such models pose new risks that regulators must understand and address.

The Commission also sent information requests to Chinese AI startups, showing the EU's rules may reach beyond European borders. Meanwhile, EU governments are discussing a digital levy mainly targeting large US tech companies as part of future budget financing.
report.impact: The EU's stance signals that AI safety is shifting from voluntary principles to enforceable regulation. For the AI industry, it means more documentation, model evaluations, incident reporting and potential fines, raising compliance costs and favoring larger firms. Developers must build safety tests, red-teaming and audit trails into their workflows, especially for frontier models. Regular users may see safer products, but also slower feature releases and tighter access to powerful models. Globally, the AI Act could become a de facto standard, influencing US and Chinese companies that serve European users. Smaller open-source projects may struggle with compliance, while regulators gain leverage over foreign AI providers.
report.tools: For compliance and safety testing, watch the EU AI Act Service Desk and the AI Act Explorer; use open-source tools such as Inspect from the UK AI Safety Institute, Garak for LLM red-teaming, and lm-evaluation-harness for benchmarking. Model cards and system cards from OpenAI and Anthropic show transparency practices. These help developers map risk, run evaluations, and document safety measures.
